en: Salutations to Śrī Vighnarāja.
Śiva said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the realization that is like nectar.
The sound struck ten times produces immediate conviction. ||1||
First is the sound "ciṇi," second is "ciṃciṇi," the third should be the sound "ciri," and the fourth is the sound of a conch shell. ||2||

The fifth is the resonance of the lute (tantra-nirghoṣa), the sixth is likewise the rattling sound (raṇavat); the seventh is the sound of the bronze cymbal (kāṃsyatāla), and the eighth is the sound of thunderclouds (megha-śabda). ||3||
The ninth is the sound of water, and the tenth is the resonance of the drum;
having transcended the nine sounds, the tenth bestows liberation. ||4||
Without being struck, the resonance (nāda) produces ten kinds of sound;
that sound, struck by the resonance, emerges from the cavity of the ear. ||5||

Having first learned the "embryonic" (garbhaka) state from the mouth of the Guru, and from that indeed the "emerging" (nirgataka), and beyond that the stainless state (nirañjana-pada), and from that the awakening of consciousness;
through the awakening of consciousness, one should always behold the supreme, stainless essential nature, which is ever-joyful— then perfection is attained.
Manifesting in fivefold forms, he sports with playful ease. ||6||
He who knows this, from the *ciṇira* wind, [attains] that womb; likewise,
through worship on the earth in a square (*caturasraka*) of auspicious yellow color,
he is not afflicted by cold and the like, nor by water, nor by the afflictions of heat and so forth.
The multitudes of diseases arising from the objects of desire remain awake as long as the body exerts itself. ||7||

When the crescent moon was formed into a circle by the chirping of the parrot, and likewise when the sound of the conch was heard, he remained in the western quarter, his intellect having perceived the inner essence of those three skillful states.
In the excellent principle of fire, within the triangular abode, in the sound of the flute, one of steady mind perceives the stainless wind within the illusory realm of Śambhu;
intent on practice by night and day, he beholds it within the beautiful red mandala.
Assuming illusory forms, he brings under his control the women of the gods and the three worlds. ||9||

When the reality arises from the wind, when there is the sound of a bell, bronze, or thunderclouds, and when the six-cornered mandala is present, one of auspicious mind should behold that which awakens consciousness. Established in the state of *arava*, he is worshipped with hosts of qualities by those who desire [liberation], within the form born of dream.
He performs the power of moving through the air and becomes a knower of the three times. ||10||

When the stainless state of existence—possessing perfectly pure qualities, arisen from one's own true nature—is perceived through the sound of the drum of the piercing of the knots (*jālandhara*), and when the impurity is seen within one's own form, the knower of yoga, who has accomplished all and is omniscient, attains dissolution into that reality which is the state beyond measure; thus born, he generates supreme bliss. (11)

These fifteen parts, which constantly cause the destruction [of the body], are those very principles (tattvas); when the mind has reached the state of union (saṃdhi), they bring about the gradual dissolution of those principles. In that body, the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet, as well as the joints, the days, and the vital breaths along with the individual soul (jīva), likewise [merge].
Having entered the family, he sports according to his power. ||12||
The earth causes destruction with five fingers, and likewise the waters with four;
fire causes drying with three fingers, while the state of space [causes destruction] for living beings.

It effects the dissolution of the principles (*tattvas*) again by two [verses], and then the Unstruck (*anāhata*) by one; it causes the drying up of the body-hair of living beings and leads them to the state of the void (*vyoma*). ||13||

He who applies himself to practice in the state of Śambhu knows the principles (tattvas); through the dissolution of those six principles into the nature of absorption, he is again established in the state of Śambhu. Through the venerable Śakti, in an instant he becomes one of equal flavor with the eternal Self; thus it truly is.
The entire sovereignty of a person arises from the grace of the Guru. ||14||
In the first [stage], one becomes beloved by the people; in the second, through the practice of *ciṇi*, there shall be the dissolution of diseases;

in the third *rāva*, one is endowed with happiness; furthermore, in the fourth *kara* and likewise in the fifth *nāda*, the wise man is joined with the attainment of the power of speech at will (*vācākāmikasiddhi*). In the sixth *svara*, he abandons the earth. (15)

The vision of the virtuous one may be distant; however, when the seventh [vision] of the sun has arisen through practice, the knower of yoga becomes like a child of the thunderbolt (Vajra) in the eighth sound. In the ninth, there is a throbbing of the body, and he becomes a self-willed lord.
When the tenth sound, Dundubhi, arises, he attains the state of equal flavor (samarasa) with the venerable Śakti and the Lord of All.

Some fortunate man, having entered skillfully through the world-renowned path, stands at the door— O, what a great battle!— fearlessly upon the ground; for by this method, through the effortless application [of practice], he indeed eludes Time, having likewise transcended the path of the moon.
He shall always sport upon the path of the sun, ever rejoiced. ||17||

At the first sound of *cīṇī*, when it has entered the skin, the glorious Lord is *ciciṇau*; when the sun reaches the blood, it is *cirirave*; when it goes to the flesh, it is *raṃmāṃsa-bhoga*; when it dwells in the fat, it is *śaṅkha-mahārave*; when it resides in the marrow, it is *svāsthitasya-ārave*; and when it enters the bone, O fearless one, it is the sound of the great conch (*mahāśaṅkha-rāva*) in the Lord. (18)
If the sound arises from bronze, it pertains to Tāla; if from a bell-metal vessel, this Lord [Śiva] is destroyed by Śukra.

Then, at the roar of the clouds, he quickly enters into the vital breaths. When the sound of the drum (*dundubhi*) is produced, he transfers it into the life-force (*jīva*) by means of the solar resonance; when the sound has ceased for both, there occurs an equilibrium of power between the two lords.
Thus ends the section on the Effortless Sound (Anāyāhatanāda).
Goddess Śivā questioned Maheśvara, the God of gods and Teacher of the World, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, regarding the knowledge of Brahman.
Śiva said:
Just as fire exists within wood, fragrance within a flower, and ghee within the essence of oil,
so too, O Lord, does the one who is free from merit and sin exist within the body.
O Dear One, Maheśa is known as the mental discipline (manodaṇḍa) consisting of the Khecarī-mudrās;
the Śāligrāma, however, is innate and worshipped by the five senses. ||3||
O Goddess Candanā, you are primordial nature; celibacy is your supreme vow.
You are the knowledge of Brahman and meditation upon it; salutations to you, the Supreme Brahman. ||4||
The *iḍā* is the Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* is the river Yamunā; one should know that between these two lies the *suṣumnā*, which is the Sarasvatī. (5)
The confluence of the three rivers is called Mastra Tīrtharāma;
one who performs an ablution there is liberated from all sins. (6)
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Existence, what is the khecarī mudrā like, and again, what is the śāṅkarī like? O Master of Knowledge, please explain both of these without effort through the realization of the inner self.

That mudrā in which the mind is steady without support, the breath is steady without obstruction, and the gaze is steady without looking [at anything], is indeed the immovable Khecarī in this world. (8)
The state of a hair, the movement of a corpse, sleep devoid of dreaming, the path and non-path of birds traversing the sky—just as these are, so is the supreme knowledge of Śiva. ||9||
The Goddess said:
O Conqueror of Death, O Lord of the World, speak to me, O Supreme Lord!
O God, why do the various philosophical systems (darśanas) speak of things differently? (10)
Śiva said:

There is a division of the three channels, and one who is always devoted to the practice of the Vedas [attains] Śaiva [realization]; there is no *bindu*, and there is increasing victory over those most terrible mantras. (11)
Those who know the doctrine of *prakṛti* are the Sāṃkhyas; the Buddhists are proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*);
and those who speak of the principles such as the non-living (*ajīva*) are the Jains, who have taken refuge in the Arhat. (12)
The nihilists, who rely on sense objects, prattle that nothing exists;
with their minds attached to the absence of happiness, they fall into the ocean of worldly existence. 13.
Thus do all those wander whose intellects are deluded by treatises;
therefore, a wise person should abandon the error of treatises with every effort. 14.
I shall tell you this knowledge of Brahman, which is even more strictly guarded than these;
by the power of which knowledge, the wonderful bliss of liberation arises. 15.
O Mahādeva, Umā asked: "What are the characteristics of the Piṇḍa-Brahmāṇḍa? O Lord, what are the twenty-five qualities resulting from the destruction of the five principles?"
Śiva said:
Bone, flesh, nails, skin, and hair as the fifth—these are indeed the five qualities of the earth, as proclaimed by the knowledge of Brahman. (17)
Semen, blood, marrow, urine, and the fifth, [feces]—these are indeed the five qualities of water, which have been proclaimed as the knowledge of Brahman. (18)
Sleep, thirst, hunger, lust, and likewise the fifth, laziness—these five are said to be born of *tejas* by those who know Brahman. (16)
"O Goddess, desire, anger, great greed, and indeed great malice—these are the five qualities of space, as declared through the knowledge of Brahman. (20)
From space arises wind; from wind, the sun is produced; from the sun, water is born;
and from water, the earth originates.
Creation arises from the five principles; within each principle, a principle dissolves.
The group of five principles is the supreme principle; salutations to that Self which is consciousness. 22.
Earth, water, fire, air, that which is known as space, the sun, and the moon—the self is supported by these eight constituents of the world. (23)
Touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing constitute the nature of the five elements; O Beloved, the mind resides within that [aggregate] as its half.
Whatever characteristics exist in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), those very same exist in the individual body (piṇḍa);
when these perish in that form, the Lord remains formless.
Semen, blood, flesh, bone, skin, hair, the channels, fat, menstrual blood, and marrow—thus the constituent elements (dhātus) are said to be of ten kinds. ||26||
The Self (ātman) is said to be possessed of a body, while the inner self (antarātman) is considered to be the mind;
the supreme self (paramātman) is other than these, wherein that mind is dissolved.
The element of blood arises from the mother, and likewise the element of semen from the father;
through the flow of the meditation on emptiness, the embryonic mass is produced. (28)
If the physical mass is not agitated, where could it perish while still existing?
Because it does not know the meditation on the embryo, it perishes. (29)
Just as there is no sleep without a dream, and no movement without thought, so too is this creator of the world; that is called "meditation within the womb" (garbhadhyāna). //30//
He by whom the mind has been brought under control and who has conquered the supreme senses has conquered the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and pannagas.
From the unmanifest, the vital breath is born; from the vital breath, the mind is produced.
From the mind, speech is born; speech dissolves into the mind. ||32||
The moon is situated at the root of the palate, and the sun is at the root of the navel;
the wind dwells within the solar part, while the mind always resides within the lunar part.
The wind moves at the tip of the mind, and the individual soul is situated at the tip of the ether;
all this is a great secret, obtained through the words of the Guru. ||34||
Śakti resides in Pātāla, while Sadāśiva dwells within the Brahmāṇḍa;
Kāla should be known as his breath, from which old age and time are born. (35)
For one in whose body Śiva always resides in a state of equanimity, death does not arise; he attains perfection while remaining within the body. (36)
When the mind is moving, there is Śakti; when the mind is steady, there is Śiva. When that [mind] becomes pure and motionless, the yogi succeeds in his task. ||37||

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and likewise the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)—these are declared to be the triad of powers. When the power of knowledge has come into being, then the mind (*citta*) dissolves. ||38||
The upward power is indeed devotion (bhakti), while the downward power is worldly existence (bhava).
Beyond these two is the stainless state (nirañjana). ||39||
The Ādhāra is located at the secret wheel (guhyacakra), and the Svādhiṣṭhāna is the linga;
the Maṇipūra is situated at the navel, while the Anāhata is in the heart.
The pure Ājñācakra is situated in the region of the throat, immediately following the earth [element].
I have described to you, O beloved, these divisions of the cakras; now hear about that which transcends the cakras. 41.
Above the throat are the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), and below are the seven netherworlds (pātālas);
this body is in the form of a tree, with its roots above and its branches below. 42.
The wind called prāṇa resides in the heart; apāna is situated in the anus;
samāna is located in the middle of the navel; and udāna rests in the throat. (43)

O deer-eyed one, the vyāna breath pervades the entire body; these five vital breaths, beginning with prāṇa, which reside within the body, are for the most part derived from primordial nature (prakṛti). 44.
The *nāga* seizes these five; the tortoise itself performs the closing [of the eyes];
the *kṛkara* causes the cutting [of the hair]; and the *devadatta* vibrates. (45)
Dhanañjaya says: One should not rest for even a moment while uttering the sound;
he who binds these vital breaths (vātas) is a yogi, the best among yogis. 46.
The nine gates are directly perceptible, while this tenth is the mind-gate; it is secret and is obtained through service to the Guru. (47)
These ten channels have become the Śakti-kuṇḍalinī;
among them, Iḍā and Piṅgalā are known as the lateral ones, while Suṣumnā is remembered as the upward-moving one.
Gāndhārī should be at the elephant’s tongue (hastijihvā), and Apū at the lower east; the two known as Alambuṣā and Jayā are situated in the right side. 49.
The two channels, Kuhū and Śaṅkhinī, are situated on the left side;
thus, the nature of these ten channels has been described by me.
Whoever knows that the seventy-two thousand channels expand into one is called a yogin by the wise. (51)
Brahmā resides in the state of *sattva*, Janārdana in the state of *rajas*, and Rudra arises in the state of *tamas*; thus, the three qualities are established in these three.
Brahmā abides in the state of compassion, Hari abides in the state of enjoyment, and Rudra abides in the state of wrath; these three states reside within the three [deities]. (53)
In the form of the *bindu* he is Brahmā; in the form of *vāyu* he is Hari; in the form of *manas* he is Rudra; for these three forms indeed reside in these three. (54)
If birth, death, and old age belong to the Self because of its being composed of the three qualities (guṇas),
then even in a dream, when one is touched by them, the Self would not be perceived as characterized by those three qualities.
The Goddess said:
Who is the father of a living being? Who is the brother and who is the sister? Who is the son and who is the wife? Tell me, O Supreme Lord. (56)
Śiva said:
Compassion is the mother, knowledge is the father, acts of hospitality are the kinsmen, one's own forgiveness is the son, truth is the wife, and a virtuous path is the home. (57)
When the bird known as "I" moves about with such certainty within the body, that state in which the foot is internalized is called the knowledge of Brahman. 58.
Whether for a moment, half a moment, or even half of that, he who attains meditative absorption (samādhi) destroys the evil produced since birth at that very instant. (59)
This is that Khecarī Mudrā; this is also that Śāṅkarī Vidyā;
and she is indeed the Mahāmudrā—the mind accompanied by the three-fold contemplation.
Other food, great exertion, idle chatter, addiction to vices, attachment to giving, and association with people—these must be abandoned by the yogi. (61)
If this living soul remains awake, whence can there be fear of death?
If the soul were always possessed of the [divine] seal (mudrā), it would be in a state of constant sleep. (62)
As long as the vital air (vāyu) remains steady in the body, whence can there be fear of death? As long as one is bound by the mudrās and āsanas, where can the vital air go? (63)
Laziness, excessive sleep, and a fickle mind—through these three, death occurs; they are considered the three causes for the destruction of success. (64)
As long as the bindu remains steady within the body, whence can there be fear of death? As long as the mudrāsana is firmly bound, where can the bindu go? (65)
He whose mind indeed moves within the void and supportless state is truly a practitioner of celibacy (brahmacārī), even if he has not abandoned women. ||66||
Without having attained sovereignty, wealth, learning, a beloved wife, or dear friends, I do not grieve;
rather, I desire only one incomparable gain: I eternally seek the reality of the Supreme Self.
[Thus ends the contemplation of the internal sound (*nādānusaṃdhāna*) in the illustrious *Yogaśāstra*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Pārvatī and Īśvara.]
